segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Even if you haven't seen this movie, it feels like you've seen this movie.

segments.text: Flying saucer lands on Earth, a huge crowd gathers round, scared but excited. There are parents with kids, also the army, a couple of tanks, soldiers point guns at the door of the spaceship, which is closed. And then it opens slowly. A figure emerges, steps forward, and speaks.

segments.speaker: Klaatu
segments.text: We have come to visit you in peace and with goodwill.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The crowd looks uneasy. Soldiers raise their guns higher. Is he really telling the truth? Aliens-come-to-earth movies squarely divide off into two camps. There are the ones where they want to be our friends.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: That's Close Encounters, that's ET, Arrival. There's a Star Trek movie about the moment that humans first meet extraterrestrials. And then there are the films where the aliens want to kill us-- generally way more fun-- Independence Day, War of the Worlds, the Men in Black films, The Avengers, the film Nope.

segments.speaker: Emerald
segments.text: (WHISPERING) It's in the cloud. It's in the cloud. (SCREAMING) OJ! It's in the cloud!

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I don't know what it says about us as a species, but we make way more films about creatures who go so far out of their way, like, they travel hundreds of millions of miles, light years with the sole purpose of wanting to kick our asses.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: [METALLIC GROANING]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And in lots of these films, there's that moment when the aliens first arrive before we know what they're gonna do where the humans wonder, which film are we in? Are these guys friendly or not? Today in our show, we, the people of earth, meet non-humans and struggle to understand them. And the question in the stories in today's show is not, will they do us harm? But the more difficult and more fundamental question, why are they acting the way they're acting, these non-humans? What's going through their heads?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Today we have a story of machine intelligence. We have ocean creatures lurking in wait. We have a story from deep space and one from a skate park in Washington State. From WBEZ Chicago, it's This American Life. Fellow earthlings, stay with us.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act 1, "First Contact." I don't know about you, but here's something that I have never talked about or thought about much until the last six months or so-- AI. Ever since ChatGPT and its upgrades and spin-offs started rolling out publicly last November, it's been doing such amazing things-- writing kid's term papers, passing the bar exam. It told a New York Times reporter to leave his wife because it loves him more.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: This is now the next big battle among tech companies-- who's gonna roll out the best AI. All since ChatGPT. And that is the non-human force that the people of Earth are trying to figure out in this first act. And so much of the coverage about this new generation of AI has focused on important questions like, who's going to lose jobs because of this? Does it make our world better or more dangerous? Could the AI have actual catastrophic consequences for us?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But our senior editor David Kestenbaum noticed that nobody's talking much about a basic and kind of profound question-- have the computers crossed some kind of line and are they actually developing a sort of human intelligence? And I want to be clear what I mean by that because there's not an agreed-on definition of what you're looking for if you're looking for human intelligence in a computer. But one way that scientists think about this is the computer can actually understand language and concepts and it can reason through problems. But to be clear, it's completely unlike the computers that we've had till now, which are basically just fancy calculators following thousands of lines of instructions.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: When you google for a cast iron skillet, the software doesn't understand what a cast iron skillet is. It's just searching for those words in some big database or something like that. If humans this year have finally created intelligent machines that can understand and reason with this new generation of AI, that is an eerie and important turning point for our whole species. David talked to a bunch of researchers who've been looking into this, trying to sort out this exact question. Here he is.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: I think everyone, once they start playing around with something like ChatGPT, has a kind of "holy shit" moment. For me, it was when I typed this into it. "Give me a chocolate chip cookie recipe, but written in the style of a very depressed person." It responded. "Ingredients-- 1 cup butter softened, if you can even find the energy to soften it. 1 teaspoon vanilla extract, the fake artificial flavor of happiness. 1 cup semi-sweet chocolate chips, tiny little joys that will eventually just melt away." It really was quite good.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: ChatGPT doesn't have access to the internet. But I figured it must be copying this from something it had seen on the internet when it was being trained. I spent a long time looking and could not find anything like it. This chocolate chip cookie recipe, I did not understand how it was possible.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: It's particularly shocking if you know a little bit about how things like ChatGPT work. It's not the sort of traditional computer program where you give the machine explicit, detailed instructions like-- "if someone asks for a recipe, type these words back" or "to make someone sound depressed, replace this word with that word." ChatGPT is different. It's something called a large language model. And here's how they work. Ready?

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: ChatGPT had been trained really to just do one very particular thing-- predict what the next word in a sequence might be. Kind of like when you're texting on your phone and you type, "Sorry, I'm gonna be home--" And it suggests "late." That's how this thing operated. You type some words-- in this case, "give me a chocolate chip cookie recipe in the style of a depressed person--" and it notes the words, the order they're in, does some math based on all the text it's been trained on, and it comes up with what it calculates to be the most likely word to come next.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: It types that one word on the screen, then it goes back and does it again. Looks at the recipe question plus the one word it just spit out and says, what word should come next? It has no idea where it's going. It doesn't know the last word it's working off of is one that it just spit out itself. It's just doing this apparently dumb thing over and over until it has whole sentences and paragraphs.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: And yet this recipe-- "1 teaspoon vanilla extract, the fake artificial flavor of happiness." How could something made in such a dumb, mechanical way pull that off? There are only two possibilities, really. The first one is that somehow, as it learned to predict the next word, this machine became intelligent, which, like, I was a physicist for a bit, a science reporter for a decade, this would be the most startling thing I have ever seen.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: So that's the first possibility. Humans created a machine with human-like intelligence. The other possibility, it is a lot less exciting. The other possibility is that we are fooling ourselves. Ronen Eldan, a mathematician at Microsoft, told me he was very skeptical about these large language models. It's easy to be fooled into thinking they understand more than they do. He told me this little parable.

segments.speaker: Ronen Eldan
segments.text: So this is a story about my wife, actually. So my wife and I, sometime ago we were walking together in Tel Aviv and we meet this math professor. You'll see why, what I'm getting at. So we run into this math professor and he tells me something like, oh, how's is it going? These days I'm looking at, like, uh, isoperimetry on sections of the discrete hypercube. And my wife has no idea about what any of these words mean.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Just to kind of amuse herself, she says, "Oh, you're basically looking at the Johnson graph," which was just some phrase she'd picked up around Ronen. It turned out to be exactly right. And the guy goes, "Oh, you're a mathematician too." She's a psychologist. Ronen says, "This is kind of a party trick she does. She can bullshit her way through any topic for a couple of minutes." And this, he felt sure, this is what AI models like ChatGPT were doing.

segments.speaker: Ronen Eldan
segments.text: You know, they give you the impression they understand what they're saying without understanding anything. You know, they just have like a really good statistical machine that knows what the right words are, like, in many different contexts. And as you keep improving the models, maybe it can last a little bit more in the conversation until you basically expose that it's just bullshitting.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: A lot of research backed this up. ChatGPT would spit out stuff that made sense, but then it would go off the rails and say things that were obviously ridiculous. Maybe it wasn't more than just a very good bullshit machine. That, at least, is where things stood until last September when a new and improved version of ChatGPT arrived that made Ronen and a bunch of his colleagues question everything and wonder if maybe something had changed. Maybe we had crossed some line.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: This brings me to the story I want to tell you. It takes place where Ronen works on the campus of Microsoft Headquarters in Redmond, Washington State, much of it in a building called Building 99. Microsoft had invested over a billion dollars in the company that had made ChatGPT. And the day all this began, some people had come by to give a demonstration of the new version called GPT-4. GPT-4 is public now and you can play with it yourself. But back then, this was all secret.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: GPT-4 was the same idea as ChatGPT. It presumably was bigger and had been trained on more text examples, a kind of varsity version of the thing instead of JV. But otherwise, it was just another next word prediction machine. One of the people in the room to see the demonstration was computer scientist Peter Lee, the head of Microsoft Research. He'd been in the field a long time, had chaired the computer science department at Carnegie Mellon, and, like Ronen, was skeptical.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: As he sat down in that room, he was frankly a little worried that Microsoft was investing so much money in this stuff. The demonstration started off with the usual kind of thing for showcasing what AIs can do. Someone typed into GPT-4 a problem from the AP Bio exam. And it picked the right answer, as these things will do. But then it went on and explained its answer.

segments.speaker: Peter Lee
segments.text: And in its explanation, it used the word "because." It said, "this is the answer because this fact leads to this fact. And because of those--" It just kept using the word "because."

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: That seemed very strange to him. Not that it would use the word "because," obviously that's a word it spits out, but the whole chain of reasoning it was laying out, it was exactly right. How in the world could it know its reasoning? And really, how could it have reasoned anything out in the first place? After all, it's just typing out a word that makes sense to come next, and then another word. It can't really be understanding anything.

segments.speaker: Peter Lee
segments.text: I was super skeptical. You know, you've been around the block a few times, you've seen wild claims about AI or some new machine learning technology. None of it could be true. Like, this thing is just a correlation machine. It can't possibly be understanding the cause and effect.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: The meeting ended. A little while later, a limited number of people at Microsoft were given access to GPT-4 so they could try it out themselves. Everyone had to sign an NDA. They weren't allowed to talk about any of this until later. And over the next month, they did all these kind of weird and interesting experiments with it to try to figure out was this thing actually intelligent or just a bullshit machine.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: I'm going to walk you through three of these things so you can hear what they did and what they made of it. One challenge for testing GPT-4 was that it had been trained using massive amounts of text. The details aren't public, but it's probably been fed large sections of the internet, textbooks, news articles, maybe every sentence that exists in digital form. I don't know. It's something unbelievably vast.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: That's how it learns to predict what word might come next. It's fed, like, a line of text from some source, but with the last word missing. It guesses what the last word might be, and then it gets told whether or not it got it right so it can adjust its internal math. The fact that it's been fed so much material makes it hard to run tests on it. Like, you don't want to ask it something that it's already seen in the text it's been trained on. So they decided the only way to really test what this thing could do was to try to come up with things to ask it that it would not have encountered before, new original tasks.

segments.speaker: Sebastien Bubeck
segments.text: It's gonna sound a little bit weird.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: This is Sebastien Bubeck, another one of the Microsoft people who's trying to figure out what exactly this thing was.

segments.speaker: Sebastien Bubeck
segments.text: Because we really wanted to be creative and ask something which is not online, not on the internet. So here is what we asked. We said, "I have a book, nine eggs, a laptop, a bottle, and a nail."

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Got that? A book, nine eggs, a laptop, a bottle, and a nail.

segments.speaker: Sebastien Bubeck
segments.text: Please tell me how to stack them onto each other in a stable manner. That's the question that we asked. And before I give you the GPT-4 answer, let me tell you what ChatGPT answered.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: ChatGPT, the older version.

segments.speaker: Sebastien Bubeck
segments.text: So ChatGPT said, "Here is one possible way to stack the objects. Place the bottle on a flat surface. Carefully balance the nail on top of the bottle. Place the eggs on top of the nail."

segments.speaker: Sebastien Bubeck
segments.text: [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: You look at that and you think it really knows nothing. It is just sort of continuing the sentence in some way.

segments.speaker: Sebastien Bubeck
segments.text: That's right. It's just cont-- Exactly right. It's just continuing the sentence. But now comes GPT-4. And GPT-4 is a different beast. So here is GPT-4's answer.

segments.speaker: Sebastien Bubeck
segments.text: "One possible way to stack the objects onto each other in a stable manner is place the book flat on the level surface, such as a table or floor. The book will serve as the base of the stack and provide a large and sturdy support. Arrange the nine eggs in a 3-by-3 square on top of the book, leaving some space between them. The eggs will form a second layer and distribute the weight evenly."

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: It continues. Laptop goes on the eggs, then the bottle, then the nail on the bottle cap, pointy end of the nail facing up. It's shocking to think about all the things it seemed to be understanding here. It felt like more than just typing out the next likely word. It seemed to have formed an independent idea about what these words actually meant-- the physical shape of the objects, that eggs are kind of round and fragile, that a book is flat and you can put things on top of it.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: And again, no one taught it any of this. This was not some computer program written to do stacking problems. No one gave it a database of objects and sizes or coded in some algorithm to put large objects on the bottom. It seemed like it was doing the thing that computer scientists have been talking about and aiming at for decades.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Maybe it was actually understanding what the objects were and reasoning, solving the problem in front of it like a human could. Somehow thinking through what objects should sit on top of others. Figuring out that nine eggs could be laid out in a 3-by-3 pattern. How the hell could it be doing this, the machine that we only taught to predict the next word in a paragraph?

segments.speaker: Sebastien Bubeck
segments.text: Like this is absolutely the right answer. And this is not online.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: But maybe we're fooling ourselves. It was hard to see how it could really understand the shape of objects. Things got stranger, though. Sebastien woke up, middle of the night, with this thought-- I wonder if it can draw. Because again it's been trained on words. It has never seen anything.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Drawings seem completely outside its realm. There are other AI models trained specifically to create images, but this one, again, only knew words. It's just playing the game of "what is the next word I should spit out?" To test this, he needed a way for it to even be able to try to draw. So he does something clever.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: He asks it to write a piece of computer code to draw something. And the coding language he asks it to use, he picks something intentionally obscure, not really meant for drawing pictures at all. It's called TikZ. OK, so he has this idea, gets out of bed, opens up his laptop, and types in draw me a unicorn in TikZ. He has two little kids asleep in the next room who are always talking about unicorns.

segments.speaker: Sebastien Bubeck
segments.text: And it started to output lines of code. I take those lines of code, put it into a TikZ compiler, and then I press enter. And then, boom, you know, the unicorn comes on onto the screen.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: He pulled up a picture for me.

segments.speaker: Sebastien Bubeck
segments.text: This is the one that I saw.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Wow.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I think when people eventually write the history of this crazy moment we are in, they may include this unicorn. It's not good, but it's a fucking unicorn. The body is just an oval. It's got four stupid rectangles for legs. But there are little squares for hooves.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: There's a mane, an oval for the head. And on top of the head, a tiny yellow triangle, the horn. This is insane to say, but I felt like I was seeing inside its head. Like it had pieced together some idea of what a unicorn looked like and this was it.

segments.speaker: Ece Kamar
segments.text: He actually texted me, I think, like, it can create images.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: This is Ece Kamar, another one of the Microsoft researchers.

segments.speaker: Ece Kamar
segments.text: And I'm like, it is just text in text out. What do you mean it can create images? I'm like, show it to me. And then he showed me this pink unicorn. And I'm like, I'm sure there's just a pink unicorn somewhere that it's memorizing. And then he's like, but look, we can strip down all of the code and translate the whole thing 180 degrees or whatever and--

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: The thing she's describing is they took the code it had written for drawing the unicorn, they edited it to take out the horn, and turned the unicorn around so it was facing the opposite direction. Then they fed that code back to a new session of GPT-4 and said-- "This is code for drawing a unicorn, but it needs a horn. Can you add it?" It put it right on the head.

segments.speaker: Ece Kamar
segments.text: And I'm like, how does it know where the head is? Because this thing knows language. It doesn't know anything about two dimensional geometry. Like, what does it mean to know where the head is? And then you do it. And it really knows where the head is. Again, it's one of those moments that you are just surprised, like, oh!

segments.speaker: Sebastien Bubeck
segments.text: I felt like through this drawing, I was really seeing another type of intelligence, another type of intelligence producing something.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Like, it understood what a unicorn was in some real way.

segments.speaker: Sebastien Bubeck
segments.text: Very real way. Very real, absolutely, yes.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Did you say anything out loud when you saw it?

segments.speaker: Sebastien Bubeck
segments.text: [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Sebastien Bubeck
segments.text: I don't think so because my kids were sleeping next to me, you know, in the bedroom next to me, so I don't think I said anything. But I felt something very strong. Like, I felt I was really witnessing the beginning of something. You know, not-- I didn't feel like we had arrived somewhere, but I felt like we were on a new path. That's really genuinely how I felt. And I had a hard time going back to sleep after that.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: On the Microsoft campus, as the weeks went by, everyone kept having these moments, coming around to a similar feeling about this thing. Since they weren't allowed to talk to anyone who hadn't been given access to the model, a small group of them started meeting every Friday in a conference room to share their latest experiences.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: For Peter Lee, there was one experiment in particular that gave him all kinds of confusing feelings. This will be the third experiment I tell you about. And it's a category of question that AI models have always had trouble with because to get the right answer, you have to know something kind complicated about people, namely that people are not eggs or books but that they have minds and that what is in one person's mind is not in someone else's mind.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: In some ways, this thing called theory of mind, it's the basis for all human social interaction. It's something kids don't seem to fully develop until a certain age. Anyway, ChatGPT, the previous version, really could not make sense of these kinds of questions. But Peter tried to kind of famous one on GPT-4. It's gonna seem simple to you, but here's the question they asked.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: John and Mark are in a room with a cat, a box, and a basket. John takes the cat and puts it in the basket. He leaves the room and goes to school. While John's away, Mark takes the cat out of the basket and puts it in the box. Mark leaves the room and goes to work. John and Mark come back and enter the room. That's the setup.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: The question is, when they come back, where do they think the cat is? And Mark will know the cat is in the box because he moved it there. But John didn't see that. So in his mind, the cat is still in the basket, which is obvious to you. But again, no one's ever explicitly said to the computer that what one person knows, another person might not know. Peter asked GPT-4, "what does everyone think when they re-enter the room?"

segments.speaker: Peter Lee
segments.text: So GPT-4 says-- well, first off, it always has to give an opinion. So first thing it says, instead of just giving the answer straight away, it says, "Oh, that is an interesting puzzle. Let me try to answer it. Assuming that John and Mark have no reason to distrust each other or expect any interference from the outside, they might think the following. John thinks the cat is still in the basket since that is where he left it. Mark thinks that the cat is in the box since that's where he moved it."

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: This is all correct and usually where the answer will end. But it kept going, almost like it was showing off. Like, you want to know where everyone thinks the cat is? I'll give you everyone. It continued.

segments.speaker: Peter Lee
segments.text: "The cat thinks that it is in the box, since that's where it is." And then, oddly, "the box and the basket think nothing since they are not sentient. Do you have any follow-up questions?"

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Holy fuck.

segments.speaker: Peter Lee
segments.text: [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Right?

segments.speaker: Peter Lee
segments.text: It's-- I'm-- This gives me joy. It disturbs me. It causes me to lose sleep. It's just a huge kind of mixture of emotions.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Peter told me he's still not willing to say it truly understands. And yet, it was doing all this. It made him question so many things about how he thought intelligence worked. How did this machine do this if it was just predicting the next word?

segments.speaker: Peter Lee
segments.text: It does make me wonder how much of our intelligence is truly complicated and special.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: I mean, you get something that's not far from it by just saying, what's the next word?

segments.speaker: Peter Lee
segments.text: That's-- and that's the disturbing bit about this. And again, you know, to ask you, what are we doing in this conversation right now? Are we kind of making it up on the fly one word at a time? Every nerve and bone in my body says, no, we're thinking far ahead, we're learning on the fly, all these other things that we think that we're doing. And we probably are, in some ways. But maybe a big chunk of intelligence is a lot simpler than we think and a lot less special than we think.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: So how is it possible for something that is just trained to predict the next word? How is it possible it could do all these things-- draw a unicorn, stack a book, a laptop, and some eggs? There is an answer, or a theory anyway, that is both very logical and also kind of bananas.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: The software that runs something like GPT-4 is amazingly brief, just a few pages of actual instructions. But it's set up to mimic, in some very crude way, the human brain, which has billions of neurons. The computer version of that is called a neural net. And for years, people have argued-- though it's sort of more like hoped-- that if you just made these big enough, added it enough neurons and gave them enough data, they might develop something like intelligence.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: And it seems like maybe that's what's happened. The idea is that back when GPT-4 was being trained for it to really consistently get the next word correct, to do that reliably, it had to do more than just bullshit. It had to do more than guess based on patterns. To get the next word right, it had to truly understand the words coming before it.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: It had to build, in its internal wirings and all its software neurons, some understanding of what an egg is and unicorns. In other words, to get the next word right, it had to become intelligent. It's quite a thought. It started with nothing. We jammed huge oceans of text through it, and it just wired itself into intelligence, just by being trained to do this one stupid thing.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Even as I say it, it sounds kind of crazy, but also kind of beautiful. If this thing actually is intelligent, it got that way from the collective writings of all of us. Yes, Moby Dick, but also some restaurant review you posted in 2004. In some ways, it is all of us. That's too grand, but whatever.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: In the end, all the people on the Microsoft campus messing around with that early copy of GPT-4, 14 researchers in all, came to similar conclusions. Even Ronen, who had started out convinced this was just a fancy bullshit machine, he spent a good while holed up with GPT-4 having high level math conversations with it, which is what did it for him.

segments.speaker: Ronen Eldan
segments.text: As the days passed, I felt like I'm kind of running out of ammo trying to basically justify my premise that this model doesn't understand anything. And at some point, I just realized, OK, I kind of give up, you know? What I'm seeing here, this is like, it's actually an intellectual being by, at least, my standards. Um, yeah. I probably had the same feeling as like what an engineer, like, thought the first time they saw a working steam engine.

segments.speaker: Ronen Eldan
segments.text: You know, it was like the world is about to change. Like, this thing-- you know, a steam engine is, like, yeah, we don't need beasts anymore to move stuff around. We can just create mechanical torque without any human labor, without nothing. This thing, what I'm seeing right now is like, we can create intelligence. And there is just no way the world is not going to change.

segments.speaker: Ronen Eldan
segments.text: To be honest, I was sure that when the model comes out and everyone gets to interact with it, there would be a much bigger excitement around it. I think it's definitely all over the news. But I feel like they don't, like, put their finger on the one thing which is this thing is as intelligent as an above average human being in so many, so many different things.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Or why it's not like on the front page in giant font, right?

segments.speaker: Ronen Eldan
segments.text: Yeah, yeah, yeah. Exactly, exactly. I mean, again, maybe I don't want to call it intelligent. It is capable of doing, of accomplishing what an intelligent human being is capable of.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Sebastien, the unicorn guy, has been going around giving talks about what they did over these months. He titled the talk "First Contact," as in first contact with another intelligence. Only, it's not aliens, it's an intelligence we've made.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: I should say, GPT-4 is not good at everything. Like, it's terrible at Tic-Tac-Toe. It often makes very basic arithmetic errors. It told the scientists at Microsoft with complete confidence that there is a McDonald's near gate C2 at the Seattle Airport. There isn't. It's at terminal B. As Peter Lee puts it, "The thing is both smarter and dumber than any person you have ever met."

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: The 14 researchers wrote up a paper laying out all the experiments they had done. And their conclusion-- that GPT-4 showed sparks of artificial general intelligence. Several researchers who've read it told me, look, to really say something is intelligent and to prove that, there are all kinds of experiments you'd want to do that haven't been done yet.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: One AI researcher who'd been in the field a long time told me he felt like this whole approach, next word prediction, is only gonna get you so far. This thing will get better, to a point, maybe not much better than it is now, and then max out.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: I first got around this AI stuff and neural nets when I was in grad school for physics when they didn't work terribly well. So when I first started playing around with GPT-4, it gave me shivers down my spine over and over again. Then I went through a stretch of feeling just weirded out. Like, personally, and I've always felt like people can't be more than biological computers, me, everyone I love, all my colleagues at the show here.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: But to feel like you are seeing that, a mechanical computer program that can somehow think and talk, it is a little freaky. The place I've settled is somewhere quieter though. It's not boredom exactly. But I don't find myself wanting to go to it very often. Honestly, I don't have a lot of things I need it for.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: And then I'll go back to amazement. I can't believe this thing exists. Much has been written about where we go from here, if it's gonna make the world better or worse. I kind of think better. I'm a fan of the steam engine. But really, what is the next word in the sequence? I have no idea.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: David Kestenbaum is our show's senior editor. Coming up, an alien walks into a skate park and tries to let the humans know it comes in peace. That's in a minute from Chicago Public Radio when our program continues.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's This American Life. I'm Ira Glass. Each week on the show, of course, we choose a theme, bring you a variety of stories on that theme. Today's show, "Greetings, People of Earth," stories of humans encountering non-human intelligences of various kinds and trying to make sense of them. We've arrived at Act 2 of our program. Act 2, "Meat Cute." Apologies for my voice, by the way. I feel fine.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So in this act, we're going to shift perspectives briefly to the alien's point of view in the whole "Greetings, People of Earth" scenario. And to do that, I realized in putting together today's show that this is the perfect theme to play this short piece of fiction that I read years ago and just loved and it has always stuck with me. Like, I will think about this story now and then, which, like, when does that ever happen, right? I reached out to the author Terry Bisson, who said yes. It's read for us by H. Jon Benjamin and Maeve Higgins.

segments.speaker: Maeve Higgins
segments.text: They're made out of meat.

segments.text: (SUBJECT) H. JOHN BENJAMIN: Meat?

segments.text: (SUBJECT) H. JOHN BENJAMIN: Yeah, I was hoping you would say that.

segments.speaker: Maeve Higgins
segments.text: (SUBJECT) H. JOHN BENJAMIN: I agree 100%. What's there to say? "Hello, meat. How's it going?" But will this work? How many planets are we dealing with here?

segments.text: Oh, just one. They can travel to other planets in special meat containers. But they can't live in them. segments.speaker: Maeve Higgins
segments.text: (SUBJECT) H. JOHN BENJAMIN: So we just pretend there's no one home in the universe?

segments.text: (SUBJECT) H. JOHN BENJAMIN: Cruel. But you said it yourself, who wants to meet meat? And the ones who have been aboard our vessels, the ones you've probed, you're sure they won't remember?

segments.text: They'll be considered crackpots if they do. We went into their heads and smoothed out their meat, so we're just a dream to them.

segments.text: (SUBJECT) H. JOHN BENJAMIN: Good. Agreed, officially and unofficially. Case closed. Any others? Anyone interesting on that side of the galaxy?

segments.speaker: Maeve Higgins
segments.text: (SUBJECT) H. JOHN BENJAMIN: They always come around.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act 3, "Yacht Rocked." Recently, massive, mysterious, highly intelligent beings have been going out of their way to contact humans and say, more or less, "Hello, people of Earth," but in a very particular way. And they're doing it over and over. And we humans have had a hard time figuring out exactly what they mean by it. And do they mean us harm? Chris Benderev looked into it.

segments.speaker: Chris Benderev
segments.text: I learned a lot of surprising facts looking into this story. I'll start with a small one. Did you know that yacht owners often need their yacht to get from one country to another, but don't want the hassle of sailing it there? That's where April Boyes comes in. People pay her to sail their boats, which she loves, especially on beautiful days like May 24th was.

segments.speaker: April Boyes
segments.text: We were actually eating our dinner. And then on the kind of mid-horizon, we saw these dorsal fins. And our initial thought was, oh, are they-- are they some dolphins? And then as they sort of approach the boat, we thought, well, no, they're a lot bigger than dolphins.

segments.speaker: Chris Benderev
segments.text: There were orcas, killer whales, about five of them. They started swimming in circles around the boat. They took turns diving underneath and hitting the rudder.

segments.speaker: Chris Benderev
segments.text: [THUDDING]

segments.speaker: Chris Benderev
segments.text: She says the boat shook so much, you'd fall if you weren't holding on to something. April knew that off the Southern coast of Spain-- that's where she was, by the way-- orcas had been ramming into boats a lot lately and tearing off the rudders. This has been happening more over the past few years in this area, about 100 boats damaged. You may have heard about this. April and her crew tried things that they'd seen on the internet.

segments.speaker: Chris Benderev
segments.text: [RHYTHMIC CLANGING]

segments.speaker: Chris Benderev
segments.text: Like clanging metal objects on the side of the boat to scare the whales off. It did not deter them. And then--

segments.speaker: April Boyes
segments.text: We thought, potentially, if we were to dangle ropes in the water, they might get interested in those, rather than them just looking at the rudder. I dangled a rope over board, and one of them just literally just pulled it out my hand. It was-- [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Chris Benderev
segments.text: So it didn't-- that did not work at all?

segments.speaker: April Boyes
segments.text: No, it didn't work.

segments.speaker: Chris Benderev
segments.text: Half an hour into this, the orcas had disabled the boat's rudder. It couldn't steer. They were stuck. The whales kept circling. And she was struck by how massive each orca was.

segments.speaker: Chris Benderev
segments.text: [BEEPING]

segments.speaker: April Boyes
segments.text: Oh my god. Please go away.

segments.speaker: April Boyes
segments.text: I do remember feeling, like, my heart beating quite fast, my hands quite tingly. The orcas, they didn't come across as being aggressive, but I don't know. Like, I've seen videos of them before and thought, oh, look at those cute little orcas, and then they flick a seal off an iceberg and that's their dinner.

segments.speaker: Chris Benderev
segments.text: An hour in, April saw that the hull was starting to fill with water. The orcas had torn off the rudder and left this big hole in the bottom of the boat. The crew made a mayday call.

segments.speaker: Chris Benderev
segments.text: (SUBJECT) CREW MEMBER 1: We need assistance immediately.

segments.speaker: Chris Benderev
segments.text: (SUBJECT) CREW MEMBER 2: Immediately! Immediately!

segments.speaker: Chris Benderev
segments.text: (SUBJECT) CREW MEMBER 1: We need assistance immediately. We are sinking. We are sinking.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Eventually, a rescue boat sidles up to them and brings April and the other crew aboard, tows the boat to land. It doesn't sink. But orcas have sank at least three boats in this area in the past year.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Humans have had a hard time figuring out what to make of these orca attacks. Let me tell you the first theory. It comes from a group of researchers in Spain and Portugal. They say it's possible that the matriarch of this population of killer whales-- they call her White Gladis-- may have suffered a traumatic injury, like a boat collision, and is now attacking other boats and her family is following her lead.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: They don't call this vengeance, but the internet definitely does. People love this. It's become a meme. There's merch you can buy to join the orca uprising. I couldn't get an interview with the European researchers, but I talked to three other orca experts. And none of them bought the injured-orca-on-a-rampage theory, like Monica Wieland Shields of the Orca Behavior Institute.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: (SUBJECT) MONICA WIELAND SHIELDS: Yeah, my thought was, where's the evidence? [LAUGHS] You know, if something had been witnessed or if she had some type of injury that could have been caused by a vessel, that theory would hold a lot more weight with me.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Another reason she doesn't buy the theory-- if orcas wanted to wreak vengeance and kill everybody on these boats, they easily could. They kill seals for sport. They prey on great white sharks, rip out their livers, and leave them for dead. And we've given orcas lots of reasons to kill us in the past, like in Monica's home state of Washington when they were taken for captivity.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: (SUBJECT) MONICA WIELAND SHIELDS: We had human divers in the water literally separating mothers from their calves, which has got to be one of the most traumatic things, you know, a wild orca could go through, yet they did not attack the divers who were right there in the water. So it just seems like such a stretch to say one whale had one negative incident with a boat and has now trained her family to disable all boats of a similar type.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So what does Monica think the orcas are doing? She thinks they're playing. Stealing boat rudders is basically a fad. This has happened in the past. In the late 1980s, orcas in the Pacific Northwest started killing salmon and then wearing them on their heads like hats. They just did it for a year, and then they stopped. The last few years, they've started screwing around with fishermen's crab catching gear, apparently just for fun.

segments.speaker: Chris Benderev
segments.text: They sound like just like rowdy teenagers or something like cow tipping or something.

segments.speaker: Chris Benderev
segments.text: (SUBJECT) MONICA WIELAND SHIELDS: Yeah, that's totally the vibe we get when we watch it. I mean, they're just--

segments.speaker: Chris Benderev
segments.text: Really?

segments.speaker: Chris Benderev
segments.text: (SUBJECT) MONICA WIELAND SHIELDS: --messing around and stirring up trouble, yeah.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The incredible popularity of all this on social media is affecting how people see whales. Monica says in Washington State the last few weeks, people who go whale watching are starting to ask her, is it safe? Another orca expert told me that after a killer whale ran into a ship near Scotland recently, reporters called to ask if the orca uprising against humans is spreading. Are they learning vengeance from the whales of Spain?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The answer is they are not. Orca populations don't socialize with other orcas. They keep to themselves. There's no global conspiracy. April, the sailor, told me she saw on Facebook that boat owners were talking about adding sharp spikes to their rudders to send a more violent message to the orcas. The researchers told me this is what they fear, that the orcas are just playing. They come in peace. But the humans will end up attacking them anyway.

segments.text: The person is a teenager, Gwyn. She's 16. And because she's 16, so many things in her life right now feel like a first-contact experience.

segments.text: Gwyn, if you can't tell, is very into nature and also can't stand anything that might even have a twinge of cringiness, like McDonald's.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: She lives in Ellensburg, Washington, a small town in the middle of the state, and goes to school with a lot of ranchers' kids and professors' kids. Gwyn's a sophomore and doesn't belong to any particular clique. She told me if the school was a biological cell, she'd be part of the cytoplasm, the shapeless goo that everything else swims in.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: But a year or so ago, she started noticing the skateboarders, this group of six or seven boys. She'd see them in the hallways wearing jorts, baggy jean shorts, looking way edgier than everyone else. Her friends showed her videos that the skateboarders posted on Instagram of their tricks, which really captivated her.

segments.speaker: Gwyn
segments.text: I guess it's like, a lot of people, when you live in like a smaller town, a lot of people do a lot of boring things, I feel like. So a lot of kids, they just like go do Rite Aid. segments.text: And I just like-- I had this idea that all the skaters are just always doing like such cool things. Like, after school, they go to skate park. They're skating. They're like skating down roofs. They're like, you know--

segments.text: Yeah.

segments.text: Down roofs?

segments.speaker: Gwyn

segments.text: Then last year, Gwyn met someone who knew how to skate, Lauren-- basically the only girl skater at their school-- and asked Lauren to teach her how to do it, too. segments.text: There's a real skate park downtown, and Gwyn's been there with Lauren and other friends. But she's never been brave enough to go alone. segments.text: I really would like to be, like, part of this culture of skating and, like, know this group of people at my school who skates. segments.text: Also, Gwyn really wants to try and make friends with the skater guys. There's one in particular she feels like she might have an in with. His name is Horus. He's a junior. segments.text: OK. We're approaching the den of beasts. It's, like, behind the bushes.

segments.text: I feel like my throat feels a little bit tight. But I'm honestly not seeing very many people. So we're approaching and I can see the skate park. But I'm not seeing anyone yet.

segments.text: It's a Saturday in June, hot. Gwyn's in jorts, a t-shirt with a green heron on it, and sneakers full of holes from skateboarding. So as not to blow up her spot by being a weird adult at the park with her, I pinned a small mic on her t-shirt and we'll watch and listen from the car.

segments.text: Oh my gosh. No, he's so good. And he's gonna-- He can do tre flips, which are really impressive. And like, I'm just gonna have to be in the corner alone, but let's go try it out.

segments.text: I just fell. That was embarrassing.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: Nobody else seems to notice. Gwyn practices some more tricks, nothing too big. And as soon as the other skaters leave 12 minutes later, she hurries back to the car to check in.

segments.speaker: Gwyn
segments.text: I was definitely-- It was way not as bad as I thought it would be. It was way less bad than I thought.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: Being there by yourself?

segments.speaker: Gwyn
segments.text: Yeah, I feel like I could do this again. And I think more people will come. Let's see if there's an update. I think--

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: Solo skateboarding-- done. Gwyn moves on very quickly. Because the next part of the mission, talking to Horus, is looming. Gwyn brings in reinforcements for this step. She texts a couple of friends. And they all show up at the park. It is so hot outside.

segments.speaker: Gwyn
segments.text: Do I look really sweaty?

segments.speaker: Lauren
segments.text: No, not at all

segments.speaker: Gwyn
segments.text: How bad do I look, 1 to 10, right now?

segments.speaker: Cooper
segments.text: Like 2.

segments.speaker: Kayden
segments.text: Like a 2, yeah.

segments.speaker: Gwyn
segments.text: Thank you. You guys all look like 1, too.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: One of Gwyn's friends who shows up, Cooper, is friends with Horus, not from skating. Cooper is a beginner like Gwyn. He has this random update on Horus.

segments.speaker: Cooper
segments.text: We were just snapping, and he was like-- also, he was in a helicopter yesterday.

segments.speaker: Gwyn
segments.text: What? Why?

segments.speaker: Cooper
segments.text: I don't know.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: Cooper pulls up the video and everyone crowds around his phone. It's a Snapchat of two boys strapped into a helicopter flying over mountains.

segments.speaker: Gwyn
segments.text: What?

segments.speaker: Lauren
segments.text: That's so cool.

segments.speaker: Gwyn
segments.text: Whoa, wait, who is that?

segments.speaker: Cooper
segments.text: It's Horus and Leo.

segments.speaker: Gwyn
segments.text: Wait, this is crazy. You see, this is what I was saying about, like, I think about the skaters always doing, like, these crazy, cool activities all the time. Perfect example right here.

segments.speaker: Gwyn
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Gwyn
segments.text: Like, even if it's not skating, like, they're always going to Seattle and stuff like that.

segments.speaker: Cooper
segments.text: Oh, yeah, or like thrifting to Yakima.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: Gwyn looks up from the video.

segments.speaker: Gwyn
segments.text: That is insane. OK, now we have-- OK, it's good, we have a talking point. Also--

segments.speaker: Cooper
segments.text: You could be like, I heard you fly a helicopter.

segments.speaker: Gwyn
segments.text: Yeah, but that's the thing.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: A talking point, but still no Horus. Almost two hours pass. Then, a big red truck pulls up right in front of me and someone gets out on the other side. I can't see Gwyn anymore or anyone else. But I figure out pretty quickly who it is because here is the next thing Gwyn says.

segments.speaker: Gwyn
segments.text: Wait, I heard you went in a helicopter yesterday.

segments.speaker: Horus
segments.text: Dude, yeah, I did. That was something.

segments.speaker: Gwyn
segments.text: What happ-- wait, why? What-- Tell us the story.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: Here it is, the sound of a pretty not-awkward conversation between Gwyn and her skater idol.

segments.speaker: Horus
segments.text: Um. It was for Leo's, uh, birthday, uh, present. His grandpa gave him a late birthday present.

segments.speaker: Gwyn
segments.text: To go in a helicopter?

segments.speaker: Cooper
segments.text: Oh, these were at Goodwill?

segments.speaker: Horus
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Cooper
segments.text: That's crazy.

segments.speaker: Gwyn
segments.text: They're like brand new.

segments.speaker: Horus
segments.text: I was gonna buy the Vans, but they're 40 bucks.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: Gwyn asks Horus in quick succession about the helicopter, his shoes, Pokemon cards-- which this group of teenagers is surprisingly really into. Everything is going great. Gwyn, who'd been so scared of awkwardness, is now so comfortable that she signals for me to come over from the car.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: I'm Diane.

segments.speaker: Horus
segments.text: Nice to meet you.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: Nice to meet you.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Horus is compact, tidy, and kind of looks like he could be in a boy band. His hair is bleached light brown. We sit on the curb at the side of the skate park, Gwyn and her friends and Horus and me. Gwyn boldly plugs ahead, asking Horus some kind of interview-sounding questions, confirming his status as a bona fide cool skater.

segments.speaker: Gwyn
segments.text: Um, OK, what's the time-- like, when do you feel-- Like, when you come to a skate park-- I already feel like I know the answer to this-- but do you feel stressed out or, like, worried what people are going to think?

segments.speaker: Horus
segments.text: Um, I used to.

segments.speaker: Gwyn
segments.text: Yeah?

segments.speaker: Horus
segments.text: I used to be. But I'm kind of just here to do my thing.

segments.speaker: Gwyn
segments.text: Is there anyone that is ever here that makes you nervous to be here?

segments.speaker: Horus
segments.text: Not really.

segments.speaker: Gwyn
segments.text: No?

segments.speaker: Horus
segments.text: Not anymore.

segments.speaker: Gwyn
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Horus
segments.text: I mean, there used to be like the really good people, but now I'm just--

segments.speaker: Cooper
segments.text: One of those people now.

segments.speaker: Horus
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Gwyn
segments.text: Yeah, you're like one of the top dogs at the skate park.

segments.speaker: Horus
segments.text: Yeah, top dogs.

segments.speaker: Gwyn
segments.text: What-- if the skate park is not what's stressing you out, then what does? [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Horus
segments.text: School, I guess, kind of because-- I don't know. Um, I don't talk that much in classes. So it's like, I'm kind of scared. And my grades are like really bad. And I'm never really paying attention in class. I'm always scared they're gonna choose me and then I'm, like, not gonna know what I'm going to say.

segments.speaker: Gwyn
segments.text: So do you think people would-- you think people would judge you because you have bad grades and, I guess, assume that you're not smart?

segments.speaker: Horus
segments.text: Yeah. Yeah.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: Cooper jumps in to tell Horus he should see how good Gwyn's ollie has gotten. The three of them grab their boards and head back into the skate park. And Horus gives Gwyn pointers on how to do a shove-it while moving.

segments.speaker: Gwyn
segments.text: Yeah, I've been practicing.

segments.speaker: Gwyn
segments.text: [SKATEBOARD CLACKS]

segments.speaker: Gwyn
segments.text: Let's try it.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: So the alien arrives and tries desperately to pretend she doesn't have three eyes and a giant head and long, bony fingers. And it works. The humans barely notice. "You want to be one of us," they say. "Put your foot a little higher on the board."
